messages.subject: Multi-level vs Multiple single-level SEMs
parts:
A bit of a silly question - what is the benefit in fitting a multi-level SEM over just fitting single-level SEMs at each specific level?

For context, I have data on viral load across several different strains of a virus (3 separate quantitative responses) in a sample of people, who are grouped into households, who are grouped into towns. I also have several individual-level risk factors (do you go swimming, do you work in an office, etc.) and several household-level risk factors (does your household store food waste indoors or outdoors, does your household employ rodent control measures, etc.)

Ideally, I'd like to determine which individual-level and which household-level risk factors have the biggest effect on viral loads for each different strain of the virus in each person (so the response is always measured at the individual level). 
  1. Option 1 is to fit a multi-level SEM (which I'm still just learning about).
  2. Option 2 is to fit a single-level SEM at the individual level and a separate single-level SEM at the household level
I realize there have to be benefits to the multi-level approach, I'm just unclear as to what they are :)

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: Multi-level vs Multiple single-level SEMs
parts: I realize there have to be benefits to the multi-level approach, I'm just unclear as to what they are :)

• Avoiding ecological/atomistic fallacies (household- and individual-level process are almost certainly not identical)
  • increased power with larger pooled within-level samples
  • individual-level variables have household-level components, so those sets of variables should not be considered mutually exclusive (e.g., larger proportion of individuals in a household who go into public spaces every day increases risk even for individuals who stay in the household)
http://quantpsy.org/pubs/preacher_zyphur_zhang_2010.pdf
